why: Must, for the count. From the opening quotation mark before "King Mongkut's prediction" to the closing one after "Art and Design." I count 906 words separated by spaces, seven of which are the double hyphens that stand for dashes, so 899 words; without the first line, 898 and 891. A second count by another route gives the same. "Some 940" is reached only by adding the bracketed attribution (11 words) and the "See Bradley" line (17): 934 by spaces, 937 to 947 if hyphenated words and figures are split. So your figure counts in two lines that are not in the quotation marks. No way of counting that I tried gives 964, so the two are not reconciled; give yours and the citation's side by side and leave it there (the citation was made from the page as it was in 2013, which I cannot see). Also must, a smaller thing: "Under the words ... it carries a passage ... in quotation marks" makes those words a heading outside the quotation. They are inside it: the opening mark stands before "King Mongkut's prediction", the line ends with a full stop and a line break, and a second opening mark stands before "In the 19th century"; there is one closing mark, at the end. It reads as the newspaper's headline copied with the piece, and it is how the citation's quote field begins. The rest is improvement, and bears on whether the passage is from the book: the passage is in entry 3928, Dan Beach Bradley (the anchor 21153 of the citation's address), a long way down a long page; the page has four attributions in square brackets, each closing a passage taken from elsewhere (Brodeur's history of Cheshire Street; the Oberlin College Archives; this one; "US Library of Congress, Bradley-Mongkut material"); the "See Bradley" line is not in brackets, is a paragraph of its own after the attribution, and is the only place where the page has "Siam Then" or "W.L.". What held: the attribution is exact as you give it, less the brackets; the pointer in full is: See Bradley, W.L., "Siam Then, The Foreign Colony in Bangkok before and after Anna," Pasadena, Cailfornia, 1981. (the misspelling is the page's), so your shortened form is fair.

why: Must. "Comes from" states a descent that nobody has traced, and the hedge in front of it hedges something else: "as far as that page shows" covers what the page is, not how the article got its sentence, and the page shows nothing about the 2021 paper. What is established is a match: the sentence on the page, less "In fact, " and "now exhausted ", is the article's sentence letter for letter but for the capital H and the two dashes (I compared the strings by script). That the article took it from this page is likely (the page is cited two sentences later, and the article's "developing chills and fever" beside it answers the passage's "developed chills and fever"), but the article's history has not been read (revisions.txt lists one revision), the newspaper has not been seen, and the newspaper's writer may himself have been following an earlier book, in which case the wording is older than 2000. "Neither from Bradley's book" says more than anyone here can know of a book nobody has seen; what can be said is that it is not the wording of the one sentence Supavit quotes. The second new sentence says outright what an editor needs for the citation: its "964-word excerpt from Siam then" and its author "W.L. Bradley" have no support on the page beyond the "See" line. The third is in your voice and must be true of you: strike it if you have in fact looked at the history.
